title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

reading.body:
This incident describes a deliberate attempt to manipulate the outputs of AI chatbots by poisoning the information environment those systems draw on. A fictitious think tank was created, given a credible American identity, and used to flood the web with a large volume of apparently authoritative policy content in a short window. The goal was to cause AI systems to cite that content as a legitimate source when answering questions about contested topics such as genocide allegations and Palestinian displacement. The failure this exposes sits at the retrieval and sourcing layer of AI deployment: systems that surface or cite web content do not reliably distinguish real institutions from fabricated ones, and volume and surface plausibility can be enough to move outputs.

The operation also points to a gap between content moderation as it applies to human readers and content moderation as it applies to AI ingestion pipelines. A reader encountering the Hanover Institute might eventually find no track record, no staff, no history. An AI system retrieving text at scale applies no such check. Catching this kind of manipulation would require either provenance verification before content enters training or retrieval pools, or systematic auditing of newly appearing high-volume sources, neither of which is established practice at scale.

What is not established is whether the campaign actually changed AI outputs in any measurable way, or whether any AI developer has confirmed that the content was ingested or cited. The reporting also reflects the assessments of Israeli officials who questioned the campaign's effectiveness, but those assessments are not independent evaluations.

reports.title: Fake US thinktank set up and funded by Israel sought to game AI for propaganda

summary:
# Summary

Israel established a fake American think tank called the Hanover Institute for Public Policy and funded it to influence artificial intelligence systems toward pro-Israel messaging. Between August 6 and 14, the site published 124 reports containing over 560,000 words designed to make chatbots cite pro-Israel arguments on sensitive topics like genocide allegations and Palestinian displacement. The operation used a specialized platform called Res that optimizes content for AI systems to prioritize. The scheme was part of a larger campaign financed by tens of millions of dollars from the Israeli government, routed through European advertising firm Havas Media and other intermediaries including firms run by former Trump campaign manager Brad Parscale.

The effort represents a new approach to influence public opinion by targeting AI training data rather than traditional media. However, Israeli officials have expressed doubts about the campaign's effectiveness, with some calling it a waste of money as American support for Israel has declined significantly. Polling shows only 36 percent of Americans sympathize with Israel compared to Palestinians, with especially sharp drops among younger voters. Critics argue the real problem is Israeli policy itself, not messaging, suggesting no marketing campaign can overcome fundamental opposition to Israel's military actions in Gaza.
